name: Design an Authentication System
intent: Let millions of users prove who they are, keep them signed in safely, let third-party apps ask for access, and withstand password guessing, stolen passwords and account takeover through recovery.
codeTitle: a slow salted hash, one-time codes and rotating refresh tokens
finalIntro: One user signing in with a password and a security key, then staying signed in.
prompt: Design the sign-in system for a service with 50 million users, like an identity provider. Users log in with an email and a password plus a second factor, stay signed in on their devices, and can sign in to other apps with it. Attackers will try every trick: guessing, stolen password lists, phishing and the 'forgot password' button.
functional: Register and log in with an email and a password
Keep the user signed in on each device, and let them sign out of one or all of them
Support a second factor: authenticator codes (TOTP) and security keys or passkeys (WebAuthn)
Let third-party apps ask for limited access with OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
Offer single sign-on across the apps of one organisation
Reset a forgotten password and recover an account that lost its second factor
Record every security-relevant event for support and investigations
nonFunctional: Store passwords so that a stolen database does not reveal them
Login takes under a second, with about 460 password logins per second at the peak
Checking a token on each API call does not call the login service
Stop credential stuffing and brute force without locking real users out
Revoke a stolen session within minutes
Treat account recovery as strongly as login itself
Keep an audit trail that an attacker with a stolen session cannot rewrite

firstAttempt.text: One users table with an email and a password hash made with SHA-256. Login hashes what was typed, compares it with the table, and creates a session id stored in a cookie and in a sessions table. 'Forgot password' emails a link containing the user id.
limits: A fast hash lets an attacker with the stolen table test billions of guesses per second on a graphics card
Without a salt, equal passwords have equal hashes and one precomputed table cracks them all
Nothing slows an attacker who tries a million passwords, or one leaked password against every account
Every API call looks up the session in the database, which then carries all the traffic
A password is the only factor, so a phished or reused password is a full takeover
A reset link that is guessable, never expires or can be used twice is a back door to every account

nodes.label: One server with a users table

steps.title: Store passwords as slow, salted hashes
steps.problem: If the database leaks, every password in it must stay secret, and a fast hash such as SHA-256 can be tried billions of times per second.
steps.fix: Never store the password. Store the output of a deliberately slow, memory-hungry hash such as argon2id (or bcrypt or scrypt), with a random salt per user and the cost settings in the stored string so they can be raised later. A good setting takes tens to a few hundred milliseconds, for example argon2id with 19 to 64 MiB of memory. Compare in constant time, and rehash with stronger settings at the next successful login. An optional secret 'pepper' kept in a key vault or HSM, outside the database, makes a database-only leak even less useful.
steps.tradeoff: A stolen table costs the attacker thousands of times more per guess, and the salt stops one cracking effort from covering all users. The cost is real: at 100 ms per hash a 16-core server does only about 160 logins a second, so the hash is the main CPU cost of login and a way to overload the service, which later steps must guard.

steps.title: Issue short-lived tokens and rotating refresh tokens
steps.problem: A session-id lookup on every API call makes the login database a bottleneck, but a long-lived token that cannot be cancelled is dangerous if it is stolen.
steps.fix: After login the token service issues a signed access token (a JWT or similar) that lives about 10 minutes, and a random refresh token. Any API checks the access token locally with the public key, with no database call. When it expires, the client trades the refresh token for a new pair, and the old refresh token is marked used. If a used refresh token ever appears again, someone holds a copy, so the whole family of tokens for that sign-in is revoked. Refresh tokens are stored as hashes, one record per device, which also gives 'sign out everywhere'.
steps.tradeoff: Reads scale with no shared state, and a theft is detected rather than silent. Revocation of an access token is not instant: it takes up to its lifetime, unless services also check a small deny list of revoked sessions. The refresh store is now a critical, write-heavy system, and about 4,000 refreshes a second must reach it.

steps.title: Defend the front door against guessing and stuffing
steps.problem: Attackers use leaked email and password pairs against your site (credential stuffing), try the most common passwords on every account (spraying), and hammer one account (brute force). A per-IP limit does not stop a botnet that sends two tries per address.
steps.fix: Put cheap checks before the expensive hash. An edge layer rate-limits by address, account and device, and scores each attempt for risk: a known device, a familiar network and normal timing are low risk, and an unknown device from a data-centre address trying many accounts is high. High risk gets a CAPTCHA or a second factor first. Check new passwords against a breached-password list, using a range query so the full hash never leaves your service. Prefer a progressive delay to a hard lockout, return the same answer and timing for 'no such user' and 'wrong password', and tell the user about unusual sign-ins.
steps.tradeoff: Most attack traffic is turned away before it costs a hash. Every rule has a price: a hard lockout lets an attacker lock out real users, per-IP limits hit offices and mobile networks that share one address, and sensitive risk scoring challenges real users. Tuning needs data and constant review.

steps.title: Add a second factor that cannot be phished
steps.problem: Passwords are guessed, reused, phished and leaked, so a correct password alone is not enough proof for a valuable account.
steps.fix: After the password, ask for something else. TOTP shows a six-digit code computed from a shared secret and the current 30-second window, accepted for the neighbouring windows to allow clock drift. WebAuthn and passkeys use a key pair on the device: the private key never leaves it, and the signature covers the website's origin, so a look-alike phishing site gets nothing usable. Issue one-time recovery codes at enrolment. Require the factor for new devices or risky logins, and for sensitive actions such as changing the email.
steps.tradeoff: A stolen password is no longer a takeover, and WebAuthn resists phishing completely. Users lose phones, so recovery must exist, and SMS codes, though easy, can be intercepted through SIM swaps. TOTP codes can still be phished in real time, and not every user will enrol.

steps.title: Let other apps in with OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SSO
steps.problem: Third-party apps want to know who the user is or act for them, and asking users to type their password into those apps would teach them to give it away.
steps.fix: The apps use the authorization-code flow with PKCE. The app creates a random verifier and sends its hash (the challenge) with the user to the provider's own login page. After the user signs in and consents to named scopes, the provider returns a short-lived, single-use code to an exactly registered redirect address. The app exchanges the code plus the original verifier for tokens, so a stolen code is useless. OpenID Connect adds an ID token that says who signed in, checked against a nonce. The state value blocks forged redirects. For single sign-on the provider keeps its own session and every connected app reuses it, with SAML or OIDC federation to a company's own directory.
steps.tradeoff: Apps never see passwords and users can see and revoke what they granted. The provider becomes the single point to be secured and kept up, redirect and consent screens are classic phishing and open-redirect targets, and single logout across many apps is only partly reliable.

steps.title: Harden recovery, and log everything
steps.problem: Attackers skip the front door and use 'forgot password' or a call to support. Account recovery is the weakest link, because it is a way in that bypasses the password and the second factor.
steps.fix: A reset sends a long random token by email, stored only as a hash, valid for 15 to 30 minutes, usable once, and tied to the account. The page shows the same message whether or not the email exists. Resetting ends all sessions and refresh tokens, notifies the old address, and does not remove a second factor. Losing the factor goes through recovery codes or a slow, notified process with a waiting period. Every attempt, success, factor change, reset, token reuse and consent is written to an append-only audit stream shipped to a separate store, with hashes chained so tampering shows, and with no passwords or tokens in it.
steps.tradeoff: Recovery is as strong as the front door, and investigators can reconstruct what happened. Hard recovery locks out honest users, who then flood support, and support staff become targets for social engineering. The audit log grows by gigabytes a day and holds personal data, so it needs retention rules and access control.

failures.impact: The attacker has every email, salt and password hash, and starts guessing offline where no rate limit can reach them.
failures.answer: The slow hash and per-user salt make each guess costly, so weak passwords fall within days or weeks and strong ones do not fall at all. Force a reset for the weakest passwords, raise the cost, rotate the pepper if it was exposed, and invalidate all sessions. A second factor means even cracked passwords alone cannot log in.

failures.scenario: A refresh token is stolen and replayed
failures.impact: The thief and the real user both hold the same token and each refresh breaks the other's chain.
failures.answer: Rotation exposes it: the second use of an already used token marks the family as compromised. All tokens from that sign-in are revoked, the user must log in again, and an alert and an audit event are raised. The thief keeps access only until the current access token expires, which is about 10 minutes.

failures.scenario: A credential-stuffing attack floods the login service
failures.impact: Tens of thousands of attempts a second each cost a slow hash, the CPU saturates and real users time out.
failures.answer: Edge rate limits and risk scoring reject most traffic before any hash. Challenge the rest, shed load from the riskiest sources first, and keep a protected lane for known devices. Scale the login servers automatically and alert on failures per account across the whole base, not only per IP.

failures.impact: Anyone can mint valid access tokens for any user, and every API trusts them.
failures.answer: Keep keys in an HSM or key service and publish public keys with key ids, so keys rotate on a schedule. On a leak, add a new key, stop trusting the old key id, and revoke sessions; tokens signed with the leaked key die at once because their key id is no longer accepted. Short token lifetimes limit the window.

failures.scenario: A user loses their phone and their second factor
failures.impact: The user is locked out, and the recovery path could also let an impostor in.
failures.answer: Recovery codes saved at enrolment are the first path. Otherwise a slow process: identity checks, a waiting period of a day or more, notifications to every contact point, and a clear cancel link for the real owner. Only support tools with audit logging can start it, and never remove a factor on one email click.

alternatives.title: Sessions or tokens

options.name: Server-side session id in a cookie
options.pro: Instant revocation and a small client
options.con: Every request needs the session store, so it is a scaling and availability dependency

options.name: Signed access token plus rotating refresh token
options.pro: APIs check tokens on their own, and theft of a refresh token is detected
options.con: Access tokens cannot be cancelled before they expire without a deny list

options.name: Opaque tokens checked by introspection
options.pro: Revocable at once, and nothing readable on the client
options.con: A network call per check, similar to sessions

alternatives.pick: Signed 10-minute access tokens with rotating refresh tokens, plus a small deny list for incidents. Use sessions for a plain website.

alternatives.title: Password hash

options.name: argon2id
options.pro: Memory-hard, which blunts graphics cards and custom chips
options.con: Needs memory per login, which limits concurrency

options.name: bcrypt
options.con: Limited memory use and a 72-byte input limit

options.name: PBKDF2
options.pro: Approved by standards bodies and in every library
options.con: Cheap on a graphics card, so it needs very high iteration counts

alternatives.pick: argon2id, or bcrypt where it is not available, with the cost raised over time.

alternatives.title: Second factor

options.name: SMS or email code
options.pro: Nothing to install, and every user has it
options.con: Intercepted by SIM swaps and phishing

options.name: TOTP authenticator app
options.con: The code can be typed into a fake site

options.name: WebAuthn security key or passkey
options.pro: Resists phishing because the signature is bound to the origin
options.con: Device loss and sync need a good recovery path

alternatives.pick: Offer passkeys first, TOTP as the common fallback, and SMS only as a last resort.

alternatives.title: Responding to repeated failures

options.name: Hard lockout after N failures
options.pro: Stops brute force on one account
options.con: Lets an attacker lock real users out, and does nothing against spraying or stuffing

options.name: Progressive delay and per-IP limits
options.pro: Slows guessing and cannot be turned into a lockout
options.con: Shared addresses are punished and a botnet slips under it

options.name: Risk-based challenge and MFA
options.pro: Targets the attacker's behaviour, and a stolen password is not enough
options.con: Needs data, tuning and the user's patience

alternatives.pick: Layer them: limits and delays for cheap filtering, risk scoring to challenge, and MFA to make a guessed password worthless. Avoid hard lockout.
